differences.title: 1. CLUSTER DISTRIBUTION
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch uses a primary-shard model with sequence numbers and translog-based durability to guarantee ordered indexing and replica catch-up. Cluster state updates drive routing decisions, and shard allocation balances based on node attributes and health.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch also follows primary-shard replication with sequence numbers and translogs. Its cluster coordination and shard allocation behavior is configurable but diverges in details: the fork introduced changes in allocation deciders, defaults, and management APIs over time.

differences.title: 2. MAPPING & SCHEMA EVOLUTION
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch’s dynamic mapping infers field types on first sight, then locks them into mappings. It supports runtime fields (in newer versions) for late binding, but indexed mappings still dominate query-time performance and scoring consistency.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch provides dynamic mappings and a similar mapping-driven indexing model. It also supports runtime fields and schema strategies, but mapping behavior, limits, and some field-type features differ, impacting how new fields roll out safely in production.

differences.title: 3. QUERY EXECUTION ENGINE
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch runs queries by translating DSL into Lucene queries, then executes them on segment-level postings. Rewrites, scorers, and caches (query cache, request cache) are tuned for common workloads and emphasize fast relevance scoring under heavy concurrency.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch similarly compiles its DSL into Lucene queries and executes per-segment, with rewrites and scorers determining final ranking. Cache implementations and some query rewrites can differ by version, changing latency profiles for complex bool/aggregations.

differences.title: 4. AGGREGATIONS & ANALYTICS
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch’s aggregation framework heavily leverages segment collection plus per-bucket data structures, enabling fast terms/histogram/date aggregations. Pipeline aggregations operate over aggregation results, with careful memory accounting and circuit breakers to prevent OOM.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch implements a largely compatible aggregation architecture on Lucene collectors, but details (execution modes, defaults, and some pipeline behaviors) can diverge. Memory breakers and internal data structures may yield different performance and stability characteristics.

differences.title: 5. SECURITY & MULTI-TENANCY
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch historically bundles more of its security story in the default distribution and uses role-based access control with index-level permissions, audit logging, and TLS support. X-Pack security controls can be tightly integrated with the stack.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch typically relies on OpenSearch Security for RBAC, TLS, and audit logging, giving a plugin-driven approach. Deployment wiring can differ (dashboards/auth, cert management), and operational hardening depends on the security plugin configuration.

differences.title: 6. VECTOR SEARCH & RAG PIPELINES
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch provides native vector fields and supports approximate nearest neighbor indexing using HNSW graphs, integrating it with standard BM25 and hybrid scoring workflows. This enables end-to-end retrieval for RAG with consistent query semantics.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch supports vector search with multiple approximation options (commonly HNSW) and exposes vector query types for kNN-style retrieval. Hybrid retrieval is available, but feature availability and configuration knobs can differ, affecting recall/latency tradeoffs.

differences.title: 7. ECOSYSTEM & OPERATIONS
differences.leftDesc: Elasticsearch pairs with Kibana for visualization, alerting, and operational workflows, and the broader Elastic ecosystem often provides cohesive UI/agent integrations. Upgrade paths may be influenced by licensing and distribution choices across the stack.
differences.rightDesc: OpenSearch pairs with OpenSearch Dashboards and an ecosystem of plugins and integrations. Operational workflows, index management tooling, and alerting capabilities can differ based on installed plugins and version alignment, influencing day-2 operations.
